sections.title: Introduction
content: Arrays and Vectors are linear data structures used to store collections of elements in sequential order.
Every element is assigned an index, making it easy to access any value directly.
Arrays have a fixed size, so their capacity cannot change after creation.
Vectors are dynamic, automatically expanding or shrinking their storage as elements are inserted or removed.

questions.question: When to Use a Vector?
questions.answer: Use a Vector when the size of the array is not known beforehand, you need automatic resizing, or you need to dynamically insert/delete elements at the end in amortized O(1) time.

questions.question: When Not to Use Arrays or Vectors?
questions.answer: Avoid them when insertions or deletions in the middle are frequent (use Linked List/BST), when O(1) search by key is needed (use Hash Map), or when memory layout needs to be non-contiguous.

questions.question: Difference Between Array and Vector?
questions.answer: An Array has a static/fixed size determined at compile-time and is allocated on the stack (or heap manually). A Vector has a dynamic size that grows at runtime, manages memory automatically, and is allocated on the heap.

questions.question: What is Capacity in Vector?
questions.answer: Capacity is the total amount of memory allocated for the vector (maximum elements it can hold without reallocation), whereas Size is the number of actual elements currently stored.

questions.question: Why does Vector resize?
questions.answer: A Vector resizes to allow adding more elements when its size reaches its capacity. It automatically allocates a new, larger memory block (usually double the size), copies/moves existing elements there, and deletes the old memory.

sections.title: Interview Rule
sections.content: If size is fixed use Array. If size changes use Vector. If insertions and deletions are frequent, consider another data structure.

sections.title: Introduction
content: A string is a sequence of characters stored one after another in memory. Each character has an index, so it can be accessed easily. In C++, std::string automatically manages its size, while character arrays end with a '\0' (null character).
Computers do not understand letters directly. They only understand numbers, so every character is stored as a numeric value.
ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is a standard that assigns a unique number to every letter, digit, and symbol. For example, 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97, and '0' = 48.

questions.question: Difference between Char Array and String (STL)?
questions.answer: A Char Array is a fixed-size array of characters terminated by a null character \0 (C-style). A String (std::string) is an object wrapper in C++ STL that manages memory dynamically, resizes automatically, and provides high-level methods like .length(), .substr(), .find(), etc.

questions.question: Why are strings immutable in languages like Python/Java but mutable in C++?
questions.answer: In languages like Java/Python, strings are immutable for memory optimization (String Pool), security (network/file parameters), and thread safety. C++ prioritizes performance and direct memory access, allowing strings to be modified in-place to avoid copy overhead.

questions.question: How does substr() work internally — does it create a copy?
questions.answer: In standard C++ STL, .substr(pos, len) creates a brand-new string object and copies the characters from the original string. This is an O(N) operation. However, modern C++ (C++17) introduces std::string_view which acts as a non-owning read-only view of a string segment without copying.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of string concatenation in a loop, and why is it costly?
questions.answer: In languages with immutable strings (Java/Python) or standard + operator in loops, concatenating strings of length L inside a loop of size N takes O(N * L) or O(N^2) time because a new string is allocated and copied on each iteration. In C++, using += or stringstream optimizes this by appending in-place.

questions.question: How would you check if two strings are anagrams?
questions.answer: You can check if two strings are anagrams in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space by using a frequency array of size 26 (or 256 for ASCII) to count character occurrences. Increment for the first string, decrement for the second, and check if all frequencies are zero.

questions.question: How does the null terminator ( \0 ) work in C-style strings?
questions.answer: In C-style strings, the null terminator \0 (ASCII value 0) is stored at the end of the character array to signal the end of the string. Functions like strlen() or printf() read memory sequentially until they encounter \0. If it's missing, they will read out of bounds, causing a crash or garbage output.

sections.title: Interview Rule
sections.content:
If working with raw character-level memory or legacy C-style code, use Char Array.

If you need flexibility, built-in functions, and safety, use String (STL).

If you need fast prefix matching or dictionary-style word storage, consider a Trie or Hash Map instead.

sections.title: Introduction
content: Hashing is a technique used to store and retrieve data efficiently by converting a key into a fixed-size integer called a hash value. This hash value determines where the data should be stored, allowing searching, insertion, and deletion in O(1) average time.
A Hash Table is a data structure that stores data as key-value pairs. It internally uses an array

sections.title: When Not To Use Hash Map or Hash Set

rows.situation: Need sorted order of keys
Need range queries (keys between A and B)
Frequent prefix search (autocomplete)
Need fast substring/pattern search at scale
Memory is very tight (avoid rehashing overhead)
Binary/raw data storage (not key-value pairs)

questions.question: What is the difference between map and unordered_map in C++?
questions.answer: std::map is implemented as a Red-Black Tree (Balanced BST), keeping keys sorted with O(log N) lookup/insert/delete time. std::unordered_map is implemented as a Hash Table, offering O(1) average lookup/insert/delete time (but O(N) worst-case) with unsorted keys.

questions.question: Why is the worst-case time complexity of unordered_map O(n)?
questions.answer: The worst-case lookup is O(N) if many keys hash to the same bucket (high hash collisions), causing the hash map to search through long chains or open-addressed slots linearly. Good hash functions and rehashing mitigate this.

questions.question: How does a hash function work internally?
questions.answer: A hash function takes an input key (like a string or integer) and applies mathematical operations (e.g., polynomial rolling hash) to generate a numeric index within the hash table's range. It must be deterministic, fast, and distribute keys uniformly.

questions.question: What is a collision and how is it handled (chaining vs open addressing)?
questions.answer: A collision occurs when two different keys generate the same hash index. Chaining handles it by storing collided elements in a linked list or bucket at that index. Open addressing searches for the next available slot in the table (using Linear/Quadratic probing or Double Hashing).

questions.question: How would you find the first non-repeating character in a string?
questions.answer: In a single pass, build a frequency map of characters. In a second pass, iterate through the string and return the first character with a frequency count of 1. Total time complexity is O(N) with O(min(N, 256)) space.

questions.question: How does the load factor affect hash table performance?
questions.answer: The load factor is the ratio of elements stored to total hash table size (n/m). As it approaches 1, collisions increase, degrading lookup performance. When it exceeds a threshold (typically 0.75), the table rehashes (doubles bucket count and re-inserts elements) to maintain O(1) complexity.

sections.title: Interview Rule
sections.content:
If you need O(1) average lookup, insert, or delete — use unordered_map or unordered_set.

If you need sorted order or range queries — use map or set instead.

If you need fast prefix matching or dictionary-style word storage — consider a Trie or Hash Map instead.

binarysearch.title: Let's Master Binary Search
binarysearch.subtitle: Learn how divide-and-conquer eliminates half the search space every step — powering O(log n) lookups in sorted data

hero.title: Let's Master Binary Search
hero.subtitle: Learn how divide-and-conquer eliminates half the search space every step — powering O(log n) lookups in sorted data
hero.accent: Cut the search space in half with every decision

sections.title: Introduction
content: Binary Search is a searching algorithm that works only on sorted arrays or collections. At each step, it looks at the middle element and decides whether the target is in the left half or the right half — and eliminates the other half.
Its main advantage is that in each iteration the search space is halved — which is why it takes only ~30 comparisons even in 1 billion elements.
A computer only understands comparisons — Binary Search uses this principle to skip unnecessary elements without even looking at them.

cards.title: Iterative Binary Search
cards.content: A search algorithm on a sorted array that repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the target with the middle element — achieving O(log n) time with O(1) space.

cards.title: Recursive Binary Search
cards.content: Same divide-and-conquer logic implemented via recursive function calls — achieving O(log n) time with O(log n) call-stack space.

cards.title: Binary Search on Answer (Parametric Search)
cards.content: A powerful variant where Binary Search is applied not on an array index, but on a range of possible answers — used when the answer has a monotonic feasibility condition (true...true...false...false or vice versa).

items.title: O(log n) Efficiency
items.description: Eliminates brute-force O(n) searches, making it critical for large-scale systems (even 1 billion elements require just ~30 steps).

items.title: Binary Search Explained in 1 Video [Theory + Code] (C++)
Not Handling Sorted Precondition
items.wrong:
// Applying Binary Search directly
binary_search(unsortedArr.begin(), unsortedArr.end(), target);
items.explanation: Applying Binary Search on an unsorted array gives wrong results with no error. Always verify or sort the array first.

items.title: Using (low + high) / 2 — Integer Overflow
items.wrong: int mid = (low + high) / 2; // overflow risk!
items.correct: int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; // overflow safe
items.explanation: If low and high are very large, their sum can exceed the maximum integer limit. The subtraction-based calculation prevents this.

items.title: Wrong Loop Condition — Misses Last Element
items.explanation: Using strictly less than (<) skips checking when the search space reduces to a single element where low == high.

items.title: Wrong Boundary Update — Causes Infinite Loop
items.wrong:
low = mid; // never moves past mid
high = mid;
items.correct:
low = mid + 1; // always makes progress
high = mid - 1;
items.explanation: Setting boundaries directly to mid without shifting by 1 can result in low and high getting stuck, causing infinite loops.

items.title: Forgetting to Track Answer in First/Last Occurrence
items.wrong: if (arr[mid] == target) return mid; // returns any occurrence
items.explanation: Simply returning mid on a match returns any occurrence. Save the matched index in a separate variable, then adjust boundaries to check the rest of the half.

sections.title: When Not To Use Binary Search

rows.situation: Array is unsorted and sorting cost is too high
Need O(1) average lookup by key
Searching in a Linked List (no random access)
Small dataset (< 20 elements)
Need all positions of duplicates efficiently
Dynamic data with frequent insertions/deletions
String prefix search / autocomplete
2D matrix with complex ordering

questions.question: What is the prerequisite for Binary Search? Why does it require sorted input?
questions.answer: The prerequisite is that the search space must be monotonic (sorted). It requires sorted input because it decides whether to search the left or right half based on whether the middle element is smaller or larger than the target.

questions.question: Why do we use mid = low + (high-low)/2 instead of (low+high)/2?
questions.answer: Using low + (high - low)/2 prevents integer overflow. If low and high are very large positive integers, low + high can exceed the maximum limit of a 32-bit signed integer, causing overflow and an incorrect negative result.

questions.question: How do you find the first and last occurrence of a target in a sorted array?
questions.answer: Perform two separate binary searches. When arr[mid] == target, instead of returning immediately, save the index as a candidate. To find the first occurrence, search the left half (high = mid - 1). To find the last, search the right half (low = mid + 1).

questions.question: How does Binary Search work on a rotated sorted array?
questions.answer: Find mid. At least one half (left or right) of the array must be sorted. Identify which half is sorted. If the target lies within the sorted half's range, search there. Otherwise, search the other half. Repeat recursively.

questions.question: What is Binary Search on Answer? Give a real problem example.
questions.answer: It is a technique where the target value is searched in a defined range of answers, and a helper function checks if a candidate answer is feasible. Example: 'Aggressive Cows' or 'Book Allocation' where we binary search the minimum/maximum distance or page count.

questions.question: How would you implement sqrt(n) using Binary Search?
questions.answer: Binary search in the range [1, n]. Let mid be the candidate square root. If mid * mid == n, return mid. If mid * mid < n, search the right half and save mid as a candidate floor root. Otherwise, search the left half.

questions.question: What is the time and space complexity difference between iterative and recursive Binary Search?
questions.answer: Both have O(log N) time complexity. Iterative uses O(1) auxiliary space. Recursive uses O(log N) space due to recursion call stack frames, making the iterative approach more memory efficient.

questions.question: How do lower_bound() and upper_bound() work internally?
questions.answer: lower_bound returns an iterator to the first element >= target. upper_bound returns an iterator to the first element > target. Both run binary search, updating candidates when the condition is met and narrowing down the search.

questions.question: Can Binary Search work on floating-point ranges? How?
questions.answer: Yes. Instead of low <= high, use a precision limit like high - low > 1e-7 or a fixed loop iteration limit (like 100 iterations) to binary search continuous real values accurately.

questions.question: How do you count occurrences of a target in a sorted array in O(log n)?
questions.answer: Find the first occurrence index first and the last occurrence index last using Binary Search. If the target is present, the count is last - first + 1. Otherwise, return 0.

sections.title: Interview Rule
sections.content:
If you need O(log n) search in sorted data — use Binary Search.

If you need O(1) average lookup by key — use Hash Map instead.

If you see 'minimum/maximum feasible value' or a monotonic condition — think Binary Search on Answer (Parametric Search).

linkedlist.subtitle: Learn how nodes chain together with pointers, enable dynamic memory, and power real-world data structures

hero.title: Let's Master Linked Lists
hero.subtitle: Learn how nodes chain together with pointers, enable dynamic memory, and power real-world data structures
hero.accent: Think in references instead of indexes

sections.title: Introduction
content: A Linked List is a linear data structure that is a chain of nodes. Each node contains two things: data (value) and a pointer that stores the address of the next node. Unlike arrays, it is not stored in contiguous memory locations — each node can be located anywhere in memory.
A computer actually understands memory addresses — it only understands numbers. Each node has its own memory address.
A pointer is like an address book. A computer does not directly find data — therefore, each node keeps the address of the next node (pointer) inside it, which we call a link.

questions.question: What is the difference between Singly and Doubly Linked List?
questions.answer: A Singly Linked List node has a data field and a single next pointer. A Doubly Linked List node has both next and prev pointers, allowing bi-directional traversal at the cost of extra memory per node.

questions.question: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list? (Floyd's Algorithm)
questions.answer: Use two pointers: a slow pointer moving 1 step at a time, and a fast pointer moving 2 steps. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually catch up and meet the slow pointer. If the fast pointer reaches the end (null), there is no cycle.

questions.question: How do you reverse a linked list in-place?
questions.answer: Use three pointers: prev (null), curr (head), and next (null). In a loop, store curr->next in next, point curr->next to prev, update prev to curr, and move curr to next. Repeat until curr becomes null. Return prev as the new head.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting at the middle of a linked list?
questions.answer: The time complexity is O(N) because you must traverse the list from the head to find the middle node. The actual insertion operation (rewiring pointers) takes O(1) time once the node is reached.

questions.question: How would you find the middle node of a linked list in one pass?
questions.answer: Use a slow and fast pointer, both starting at the head. Move the slow pointer 1 step and the fast pointer 2 steps per iteration. When the fast pointer reaches the end (null or fast->next == null), the slow pointer will be at the middle.

questions.question: How does a linked list differ from an array in terms of memory layout?
questions.answer: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory slots, allowing O(1) index-based access. Linked Lists allocate nodes dynamically in scattered memory, connected by pointers. Traversal is O(N), but insertion/deletion is O(1) once pointers are located.

sections.title: Interview Rule
sections.content:
If you need O(1) insert/delete at head or tail — use Linked List.

If you need O(1) random access by index — use Array or Vector instead.

If you need bidirectional traversal or O(1) deletion given a node pointer — use Doubly Linked List.

hero.subtitle: Learn LIFO processing, monotonic stacks and expression handling

sections.title: Introduction
content: A Stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last In First Out) principle.
This means that the element inserted last (Push) will be the first one to be removed (Pop).
In a Stack, both insertion and deletion operations are performed from only one end, called the Top.
When a new element is added, it is added at the Top, and when an element is removed, it is also removed from the Top.

sections.title: One Line Definition
sections.content: A Stack is a data structure where insertion and deletion happen from only one side, called the Top.

items.title: Why Stack?

questions.question: What is the LIFO principle and where is it used in computer systems?
questions.answer: LIFO (Last In First Out) means the element inserted last is the first to be removed. It is used in call stack management (function calls/recursion), undo/redo mechanisms, syntax parsing, and browser history navigation.

questions.question: How do you implement a stack using queues?
questions.answer: You can implement a stack using two queues. To keep push O(1), make pop O(N) by shifting all elements but one from the active queue to the helper queue, removing the last one, and swapping roles. Alternatively, make push O(N) by reversing order on insertion.

questions.question: What is a monotonic stack and when should you use it?
questions.answer: A monotonic stack is a stack that maintains its elements in a strictly increasing or decreasing order. Use it to solve Next Greater Element, Daily Temperatures, or Largest Rectangle in Histogram in linear O(N) time.

questions.question: How is a stack used in expression evaluation (Infix, Prefix, Postfix)?
questions.answer: Stacks store operators or operands. In Postfix evaluation, scan left to right: push operands; pop two, evaluate, and push result when encountering an operator. In Infix parsing (Shunting-yard), stacks manage operator precedence.

questions.question: What is the difference between Stack Overflow and Stack Underflow?
questions.answer: Stack Overflow occurs when the stack grows beyond its allocated memory limit (common in deep recursion). Stack Underflow occurs when you attempt to pop or peek from an empty stack.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of push, pop, and peek operations on a stack?
questions.answer: All three operations (push, pop, peek) have O(1) time complexity because they only interact with the top of the stack and do not require traversing the rest of the elements.

sections.title: Introduction
content: A Queue is a linear data structure that follows the FIFO (First In First Out) principle.
This means that the element inserted first (Enqueue) will be the first one to be removed (Dequeue).
In a Queue, insertion happens at one end called the Rear (Back), and deletion happens at the other end called the Front.
When a new element is added, it is added at the Rear, and when an element is removed, it is removed from the Front.

questions.question: What is the FIFO principle and how does it differ from LIFO?
questions.answer: FIFO (First In First Out) means the first element inserted is the first to be removed. It differs from LIFO (where the last element goes out first). It represents a standard waiting line where service is sequential.

questions.question: How do you implement a queue using stacks?
questions.answer: Use two stacks: input and output. Push elements to input. For pop/peek, if output is empty, pop all elements from input and push them to output (reversing order). Then, pop/peek from output. This achieves O(1) amortized cost.

questions.question: What is a Deque (Double-ended Queue) and when is it useful?
questions.answer: A Deque is a sequence container that supports fast O(1) insertion and deletion at both its front and back. It is useful in sliding window maximum problems, custom buffers, and job stealing algorithms.

questions.question: Why is Queue preferred over Stack for BFS traversal?
questions.answer: BFS traverses level-by-level, exploring all nodes at distance D before distance D+1. A Queue preserves this order (FIFO). A Stack would reverse it (LIFO), resulting in a Depth-First Search (DFS) behavior.

questions.question: What is a Circular Queue and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: A Circular Queue is a linear queue where the last position is connected back to the first. It solves the memory wastage problem of a standard array-based queue, where dequeued spaces cannot be reused because the rear pointer reaches the end.

questions.question: What is a Priority Queue and how is it implemented internally?
questions.answer: A Priority Queue is an abstract data type where each element has a priority, and elements are served based on priority. It is typically implemented internally using a Binary Heap (Max-Heap or Min-Heap) supporting O(log N) push/pop.

sections.title: Introduction
content: A Tree is a non-linear, hierarchical data structure in which nodes are connected in parent-child relationships. The topmost node is called the 'root', and each node can have zero or more 'children' below it — just like a family tree.
In a Linked List, each node pointed to only one next node, but in a Tree, a node can point to multiple children — creating a branching structure.

Each node with no children is called a 'leaf node', and the longest path from the root to any leaf is called the 'height'. This structure is perfect for searching, sorting, and representing hierarchical data (like file systems or org charts).

questions.question: What is the difference between a Binary Tree and a Binary Search Tree?
questions.answer: A Binary Tree only restricts each node to at most two children, with no ordering rule. A Binary Search Tree additionally requires that the left subtree's values are smaller and the right subtree's values are larger than the node itself.

questions.question: How do you find the height of a binary tree?
questions.answer: Recursively compute 1 + max(height(left subtree), height(right subtree)), with the base case returning 0 for a null node.

questions.question: How do you check if a binary tree is balanced?
questions.answer: For every node, compute the height of the left and right subtrees. If the absolute difference is more than 1 at any node, or any subtree is unbalanced, the tree is not balanced. This is usually done bottom-up in a single traversal for O(n) efficiency.

questions.question: What is the difference between inorder, preorder, and postorder traversal?
questions.answer: Inorder visits Left → Node → Right (gives sorted order for a BST). Preorder visits Node → Left → Right (useful for copying a tree). Postorder visits Left → Right → Node (useful for safely deleting a tree).

questions.question: How do you find the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of two nodes in a BST?
questions.answer: Starting at the root, if both values are smaller than the current node, recurse left. If both are larger, recurse right. The moment the values split (one smaller, one larger, or one equals the node), that node is the LCA.

questions.question: Why can BST operations degrade to O(n)?
questions.answer: If elements are inserted in sorted (or reverse sorted) order, the BST becomes skewed like a linked list, with each node having only one child. This removes the benefit of branching, making search, insert, and delete all O(n) instead of O(log n).

sections.title: Interview Rule
sections.content:
If you need fast ordered search, insert, and delete — use a Binary Search Tree.

If worst-case O(log n) guarantees matter — use a self-balancing tree like AVL or Red-Black Tree.

If you only need key-value lookups with no ordering requirement — use a Hash Map instead.

hero.title: Let's Master Heaps & Priority Queues
hero.subtitle: Learn how a complete binary tree gives instant access to the min or max element, and powers scheduling systems everywhere

sections.title: Introduction
content: A Heap is a special complete binary tree stored in an array that follows a simple rule: in a Min-Heap, each parent is smaller than its children, and in a Max-Heap, each parent is larger than its children.

Since a Heap is a 'complete' tree (every level except the last is fully filled), we can store it in a simple array — no explicit left/right pointers needed. Parent and children indices are calculated by formulas: parent = (i-1)/2, left = 2i+1, right = 2i+2.
A Priority Queue is an abstract data type that always extracts the highest-priority element first — and a Heap is its most efficient real-world implementation, with O(log n) insertion and O(1) peek.

center.description: When we search for the cheapest flight, we repeatedly need the 'lowest price so far'. A Min-Heap always keeps the smallest value at the root — which is why shortest-path problems like Dijkstra's algorithm are based on it.

right.title: Priority Queue — OS Task Scheduler
right.description: In an Operating System, the CPU scheduler runs tasks based on their priority, not the order they arrived. A high-priority task (like a system alert) will run before a low-priority background task — this is a classic real-world use case of a Priority Queue.

explanation: Unlike Linked Lists or Trees, a Heap is stored in a single contiguous array — there are no pointers at all. Parent and child relationships are derived purely from index arithmetic.
For any node at index i: parent is at (i-1)/2, left child is at 2i+1, right child is at 2i+2. This makes a Heap extremely cache-friendly compared to pointer-based tree structures.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Heap and a Priority Queue?
questions.answer: A Heap is a concrete data structure (a complete binary tree stored as an array). A Priority Queue is an abstract data type that serves elements by priority — Heaps are simply the most common and efficient way to implement it.

questions.question: How do you find the Kth largest element in an array using a heap?
questions.answer: Maintain a Min-Heap of size K. Iterate through the array, pushing each element; if the heap size exceeds K, pop the smallest. After processing all elements, the root of the heap is the Kth largest element.

questions.question: How is a Heap represented using an array instead of pointers?
questions.answer: Because a heap is always a complete binary tree, its nodes can be stored level by level in an array. For any index i, its parent is at (i-1)/2, its left child is at 2i+1, and its right child is at 2i+2 — no explicit pointers are needed.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of building a heap from an unsorted array, and why is it O(n) and not O(n log n)?
questions.answer: Although each heapifyDown call can take O(log n), most nodes are near the bottom of the tree where heapify does very little work. Summing the work across all levels gives a tighter bound of O(n) rather than O(n log n).

questions.question: How would you find the median of a running stream of numbers?
questions.answer: Use two heaps: a Max-Heap for the smaller half of the numbers and a Min-Heap for the larger half, keeping their sizes balanced. The median is either the top of the larger heap, or the average of both tops if sizes are equal.

questions.question: Why is Heap Sort not a stable sorting algorithm?
questions.answer: Heap Sort repeatedly swaps the root with the last element and sifts down, which can change the relative order of equal elements during these swaps, so it does not preserve the original order of duplicates.

sections.title: Interview Rule
sections.content:
If you need instant access to the smallest or largest element — use a Heap.

If you need elements served strictly by priority rather than arrival order — use a Priority Queue (backed by a Heap).

If you need fully sorted order or fast arbitrary search — use a Balanced BST or Sorted Array instead.

sections.title: Introduction
content: A Graph is a non-linear data structure composed of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections). Unlike trees, a Graph has no fixed 'root' and a node can connect to any number of other nodes — even in a cycle.

Edges can be of two types: directed (one-way connections, like an Instagram follow) or undirected (two-way connections, like a Facebook friendship). Edges can also have weights, representing cost, distance, or time.

Graphs are best for modeling real-world relationships — social networks, maps/roads, computer networks, and dependency chains (like build systems) — where the connection pattern does not follow a predictable, tree-like hierarchy.

explanation: Graphs are usually stored as an adjacency list (array/map of lists, one per vertex holding its neighbors) or an adjacency matrix (a V x V grid of 0s/1s marking edges).
Adjacency list uses O(V+E) space and is fast for sparse graphs (traversal-friendly). Adjacency matrix uses O(V^2) space but gives O(1) edge-existence checks — better for dense graphs.

items.explanation: Without a visited set, DFS/BFS on a graph with a cycle will revisit the same nodes endlessly, causing an infinite loop or stack overflow.

items.title: Treating a Directed Graph as Undirected
items.explanation: Adding the reverse edge by default silently turns a directed graph into an undirected one, breaking algorithms like topological sort that rely on edge direction.

items.title: Using DFS Visited-Only Check for Cycle Detection in Directed Graphs
items.explanation: In a directed graph, a plain visited check flags valid cross-edges as cycles. You need a separate recursion-stack tracker to detect true back edges.

Need O(1) random access by index
Need fast key-value lookups with no relationships
Data is purely sequential with no branching
Relationships are simple parent-child only
Extremely large dense graphs with memory constraints
rows.choice: Compressed adjacency structures or specialized graph databases

questions.question: What is the difference between BFS and DFS?
questions.answer: BFS explores level by level using a queue, ideal for shortest path in unweighted graphs. DFS explores as deep as possible using recursion or a stack before backtracking, better suited for cycle detection and topological sort.

questions.question: What is the difference between an adjacency list and an adjacency matrix?
questions.answer: An adjacency list stores only existing edges as a list per vertex, using O(V+E) space and favoring sparse graphs. An adjacency matrix stores a V x V grid marking all possible edges, using O(V^2) space but giving O(1) edge lookups, favoring dense graphs.

questions.question: How do you detect a cycle in an undirected graph?
questions.answer: Run DFS while tracking the parent of each node. If you visit a node that is already visited and it is not the immediate parent, a cycle exists. Union-Find is also commonly used for this.

questions.question: What is topological sort and when can it be applied?
questions.answer: Topological sort orders vertices so that every directed edge points from an earlier vertex to a later one. It can only be applied to a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — a directed graph with no cycles.

questions.question: How does Dijkstra's algorithm find the shortest path?
questions.answer: Dijkstra's uses a min-priority queue to repeatedly pick the unvisited vertex with the smallest known distance, then relaxes (updates) the distances of its neighbors. It works only on graphs with non-negative edge weights.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Graph and a Tree?
questions.answer: A Tree is a special case of a Graph that is connected, acyclic, and has exactly one path between any two nodes (N nodes, N-1 edges). A Graph has no such restrictions — it can have cycles, multiple paths, disconnected parts, or multiple parents per node.

sections.title: Interview Rule
sections.content:
If you need shortest path in an unweighted graph — use BFS.

If you need cycle detection, topological sort, or deep exploration — use DFS.

If edges have weights and you need the cheapest path — use Dijkstra's (non-negative weights) or Bellman-Ford (handles negative weights).
